meta.title: Diversity of Matter: Atoms and the Periodic Table
meta.subject: Science

learningOutcomes: By the end, you can name the sub-atomic particles, say where they are and state their charges.
By the end, you can describe the atomic number and the mass number, and find the protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom.
By the end, you can explain how the periodic table is arranged and use it to read the atomic number of an element.
By the end, you can write and draw electron arrangements, explain how ions form and describe a molecule.

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: The mass number is the same as the atomic number.
misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: The atomic number counts protons only. The mass number counts protons plus neutrons.

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: Neutrons are found by adding Z and A.
misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: Neutrons = mass number minus atomic number.

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: The periodic table is in alphabetical order.
misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: It follows the atomic number, the number of protons.

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: Electrons fill the outer shell first.
misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: The shell nearest the nucleus fills first.

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: Forming an ion changes the number of protons.
misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: Only electrons are gained or lost. The protons stay the same.

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: A molecule must have different kinds of atoms.

narration.script: Atoms are made of sub-atomic particles: protons, electrons and, in most atoms, neutrons. Protons and neutrons are found together in the centre of the atom, called the nucleus. Electrons move around the nucleus in regions called shells. The most common hydrogen atom has one proton and one electron and no neutron. The nucleus is tiny, but it holds almost all of the mass of the atom.

narration.ttsText: Atoms are made of sub-atomic particles: protons, electrons and, in most atoms, neutrons. Protons and neutrons are found together in the centre of the AT-um, called the NYOO-klee-us. Electrons move around the NYOO-klee-us in regions called shells. The most common hydrogen AT-um has one PROH-ton and one ih-LEK-tron and no NYOO-tron. The NYOO-klee-us is tiny, but it holds almost all of the mass of the AT-um.

keyIdeas: The sub-atomic particles are protons, neutrons and electrons.

narration.script: Look at this model of an atom, lithium-7. The nucleus is at the centre and contains 3 protons and 4 neutrons. The 3 electrons are in shells around the nucleus, 2 in the first shell and 1 in the second, so the electron configuration is 2, 1. This is a simple model: real electrons do not travel in neat circles, but the model helps us count and arrange them.

narration.script: The rows of the periodic table are called periods, and the columns are called groups. Elements in the same group have similar properties. For example, lithium, sodium and potassium are alkali metals in Group 1, and they are soft metals that react strongly with water. Hydrogen sits at the top of the first column in this simplified table, but it is a non-metal gas, not a Group 1 metal. The period number also tells us how many shells the atoms have.

narration.script: The way electrons are arranged in shells is called the electron configuration. Each shell can hold only a certain number of electrons. For the first twenty elements we use a simplified school pattern: up to two electrons in the first shell, up to eight in the second, and eight in the third before the fourth shell starts. Electrons fill the shell nearest the nucleus first. This is a simplified pattern for these elements, and it is not a rule for all atoms.
pauseCues: after 'The way electrons are arranged in shells is called the electron configuration.'
narration.ttsText: The way electrons are arranged in shells is called the ih-LEK-tron kun-fig-yuh-RAY-shun. Each shell can hold only a certain number of electrons. For the first twenty elements we use a simplified school pattern: up to two electrons in the first shell, up to eight in the second, and eight in the third before the fourth shell starts. Electrons fill the shell nearest the NYOO-klee-us first. This is a simplified pattern for these elements, and it is not a rule for all atoms.

keyIdeas: The arrangement of electrons in shells is the electron configuration.

narration.script: Here is how to write the electron configuration of an atom. First, find the number of electrons, which is the same as the atomic number for a neutral atom. Second, put up to two electrons in the first shell. Third, put up to eight in the second shell. Last, put the remaining electrons in the third shell, using the simplified school pattern, and then the fourth shell. For example, carbon has six electrons, so its electron configuration is two, four.

Last, put the remaining electrons in the third shell, using the simplified school pattern, and then the fourth shell. For example, carbon has six electrons, so its ih-LEK-tron kun-fig-yuh-RAY-shun is two, four.

narration.script: An atom can gain or lose electrons, and then it becomes an ion. An ion is a particle with an overall electrical charge. Atoms do this to get a full, stable outer shell, like the noble gases helium, neon and argon. If an atom loses electrons, it has more protons than electrons, so it becomes a positive ion, called a cation. If it gains electrons, it becomes a negative ion, called an anion. The number of protons does not change.

narration.ttsText: An AT-um can gain or lose electrons, and then it becomes an EYE-on. An EYE-on is a particle with an overall electrical charge. Atoms do this to get a full, stable outer shell, like the noble gases helium, neon and argon. If an AT-um loses electrons, it has more protons than electrons, so it becomes a positive EYE-on, called a KAT-eye-un. If it gains electrons, it becomes a negative EYE-on, called an AN-eye-un. The number of protons does not change.

keyIdeas: An ion is a charged particle.
A cation is a positive ion and an anion is a negative ion.
Atoms gain or lose electrons to get a full outer shell.

interactive.instructions: Select any ionic compound below (NaCl, MgO, MgCl₂, CaCl₂, Al₂O₃). Adjust metal and non-metal atom counts and transfer outer electrons so every ion reaches a full outer shell and net charge equals zero in the simplest whole-number ratio.

examples.label: MgO (1:1)

examples.label: CaCl₂ (1:2)

examples.successExplanation: 2 Al³⁺ (+6) and 3 O²⁻ (−6) balance after transferring 6 electrons in total (Al₂O₃).

narration.script: Let us recap. An atom is made of protons and neutrons in the nucleus, with electrons in shells around it. Protons are positive, electrons are negative and neutrons have no charge. The atomic number is the number of protons, and the mass number is protons plus neutrons. The periodic table arranges the elements by atomic number, and the electron configuration shows how the electrons fill the shells. Atoms can gain or lose electrons to form cations and anions, and atoms can join to form molecules.

The peer-ee-OD-ik TAY-bul arranges the elements by atomic number, and the ih-LEK-tron kun-fig-yuh-RAY-shun shows how the electrons fill the shells. Atoms can gain or lose electrons to form cations and anions, and atoms can join to form molecules.

keyIdeas: An atom has protons, neutrons and electrons.
The periodic table is in order of atomic number.
Atoms form ions by gaining or losing electrons, and molecules by joining.

summary.recapScript: An atom has protons and neutrons in the nucleus and electrons in shells around it. A proton is positive, an electron is negative and a neutron has no charge. The atomic number is the number of protons, and the mass number is the protons plus the neutrons. The periodic table arranges the elements in order of atomic number. Electrons fill the shells in the order two, eight, eight. Atoms that gain or lose electrons form ions, and atoms that join together form molecules.
takeaways: An atom has a nucleus with protons and neutrons, and electrons in shells.
The atomic number is the number of protons, and neutrons = A minus Z.
Ions form when electrons are gained or lost, and molecules form when atoms join.

extensionActivity.title: Build an Atom Model
materials: Bottle tops or beads in three colours
A sheet of paper or card
A ruler and a pair of compasses or a round plate to trace
steps: Your teacher gives you one atom from the first 20 elements, together with its mass number, for example carbon-12 or sodium-23. Find the atomic number in the periodic table and write both numbers in your book. The atomic number alone does not tell you the neutrons; you need the mass number.
Work out the number of protons, electrons and neutrons (neutrons = mass number minus atomic number), and write them down.
Draw a nucleus in the centre of the paper and place one colour of bottle tops for the protons and another for the neutrons.
Draw the electron shells around the nucleus and place the third colour on the shells for the electrons, filling shell 1 first.
Write the electron configuration under your drawing, for example 2, 8, 1 for sodium, and name the valence electrons in the outer shell.
Swap models with a partner. Check each other's counts, then write one sentence saying how an ion of the same element would differ.
extensionActivity.safetyNote: Use only clean, safe items such as bottle tops, beads and paper. Keep small items away from the mouth and do not put them in your ears or nose. Tidy up all items at the end, and wash your hands afterwards.
